Exped Ultra -10°C | 15°F Sleeping Bag Review — Warmth Without the Bulk

by Max DesMarais

Article Categories: Gear
Article Tags: Backpacking Gear | Camping Gear

Table Of Contents

  • Real-World Testing
  • What Makes This Bag Stand Out

Instaread

Finding a sleeping bag that genuinely performs at its rated temperature without weighing down your pack or making you feel like you’re sleeping in a straightjacket is harder than it sounds. A lot of bags either run cold, run heavy, or sacrifice room to move just to hit a weight number on a spec sheet.

After seven nights in the Exped Ultra -10°C | 15°F, across car camping trips and a shoulder-season backpacking outing, I came away impressed. This bag delivers serious cold-weather warmth in a package that still compresses down small enough to carry on the trail.

 

Where To Buy

  • Buy from Exped USA
  • Buy from REI

 

Real-World Testing

I put this bag through seven total nights across a mix of car camping and backpacking, in temperatures ranging from the low 30s up into the mid-50s Fahrenheit:

  • 3 nights car camping in Southern Utah
  • 2 nights car camping in Fruita, Colorado
  • 1 night backpacking in the Uinta WIlderness
  • 1 night backpacking in the Wasatch Mountains

Most of these nights were spent cowboy camping, as I hate climbing in and out of a small tent if I don’t have to. I think it makes for an honest assessment of a sleeping bag as well. 

The standout night was camping in the desert outside Hanksville, Utah, in wind gusts up to 30 mph. Temperatures dropped into the low 30s, and I slept completely warm and comfortable in nothing but shorts and a t-shirt. 

 

What Makes This Bag Stand Out

 

Warmth That Holds Up in Real Conditions

The Ultra’s 850+ fill power down does exactly what it’s supposed to do. Even with strong wind working against me in the desert, I never felt a cold spot or a draft creeping in.

For a bag rated to 15°F comfort, performing this well in gusty 30-degree conditions is a strong sign the rating isn’t inflated.

 

Long Wide Sizing That Actually Fits

I’m 6’4″, and fit is usually where sleeping bags let me down. I went with the Long Wide version, and it was the right call. There’s enough room inside to roll over, shift positions, and stretch out without feeling boxed in, which makes a real difference on longer trips when you’re not just sleeping, you’re trying to actually rest.

 

A Footbox Roomy Enough to Double as a Locker

The 3D footbox isn’t just about comfort for your feet. It’s large enough that I could stash my next day’s clothes down there overnight, so I’d wake up to a warm set of clothes. It’s a small thing, but it’s the kind of detail that makes cold mornings noticeably better.

 

Packs Down Well for a Bag This Warm

This isn’t an ultralight bag, and it’s not trying to be. But for the warmth it provides, the included stuff sack compression is excellent. On my Uintas trip, it compressed down small enough to sit comfortably at the bottom of my pack without eating up the space I needed for everything else.

 

Performance Across Activities

 

Car Camping

This is where the bag shines without much effort. Across six nights of car camping in Southern Utah, Fruita, and the Wasatch, it handled everything from chilly desert wind to warm Colorado nights without issue.

In Fruita, temperatures ran warm enough that I ended up using the bag unzipped and draped over me like a quilt rather than fully cinched up. That flexibility, being able to dump excess warmth on a hot night, is a nice bonus for a bag built primarily for cold weather.

 

Shoulder-Season Backpacking

On the two backpacking trips so far with overnight temps dipping into the low 30s, the Ultra kept me perfectly warm. Combined with how well it compresses, it’s a strong choice for anyone backpacking into fall or early spring conditions where a 3-season bag might leave you cold.

 

Downsides

Seven nights in, there’s honestly not much to complain about:

  • Not a true ultralight bag. If you’re chasing the lightest possible base weight, there are bags that shave more ounces, though you’ll likely be giving up some warmth or durability to get there.
  • Overkill for warm summer nights. As the Fruita trip showed, this bag is happiest below 50°F. On warmer nights you’ll be using it more like a blanket than a sleeping bag.

 

Who This Bag Is For

  • Car campers who want reliable warmth down into the 20s and 30s
  • Shoulder-season backpackers heading into fall or early spring conditions
  • Taller campers who want room to move without sizing into a bulkier bag
  • Anyone who cowboy camps and wants a bag that performs without a tent’s added warmth

 

Who It Might Not Be For

  • Ultralight backpackers prioritizing the lowest possible pack weight above all else
  • Summer-only campers who don’t need a bag rated this warm
  • Campers on a tight budget, as this sits at a premium price point

 

Specifications

Product Name Exped Ultra -10°C | 15°F (Long Wide)
Type Down mummy sleeping bag
Primary Use Car camping, shoulder-season backpacking
Temperature Rating Comfort: 28°F · Limit: 18°F · Extreme: -15°F
Weight (LW) 2 lbs 11 oz (5 total sizes available)
Fits Up To 6’5″
Shoulder Girth (LW) 65 in
Sleeping Bag Length (LW) 86 in
Packed Dimensions (LW) 6.7 x 8.7 x 10.6 in
Fill 850+ cuin/oz White Muscovy Duck Down, RDS certified
Shell/Liner Recycled 10D/15D ripstop nylon
Includes Sleeping bag, mesh storage bag, waterproof drybag
Price $499.95

 

Final Thoughts

The Exped Ultra -10°C | 15°F is a bag that does exactly what its rating promises, and then some. After seven nights spread across desert wind, high-country cold, and warm valley camping, it never once let me down on warmth, and the Long Wide sizing finally gave me room to actually move at night instead of fighting the bag.
